## Google Play closed testing requirements: the complete 2026 guide
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/google-play-closed-testing-requirements/

If you opened a personal Google Play developer account after 13 November 2023, you can't publish straight to production. Google first wants a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for at least 14 days in a row. Then you fill in a short production access form and wait for Google's review. This guide explains every part of the rule as Google states it in the Play Console Help Center, what actually trips developers up, and a realistic timeline from first upload to public release.

### Who has to do closed testing

Google's Help Center says the requirement applies to personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023. Until those apps pass it, they are not eligible for distribution on Google Play.

If your account was created before that date, or it is an organization account (a business verified with a D-U-N-S number), the closed testing requirement does not apply to you. Each app on an affected personal account goes through the process before it gets production access.

- Personal account, created after 13 Nov 2023: closed test required.
- Personal account, created before 13 Nov 2023: not required.
- Organization account: not required, but you need a D-U-N-S number and a verified organization website. See the guide on organization vs personal accounts.

### The rule in one sentence

Run a closed test with at least 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days, then apply for production access from the Play Console Dashboard.

Google's wording matters. The 14 days must be consecutive. Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out do not count. And at least 12 testers must still be opted in on the day you apply.

The number was 20 testers until December 2024, when Google lowered it to 12. The 14 days did not change.

### What counts as a tester

- A real Google Account that opted in. Being on your email list or in your Google Group is not enough. Each person has to open the opt-in link and tap to become a tester.
- On the closed track. People who opted into your internal test are not eligible for closed tests until they leave the internal test. Internal testing does not count toward the requirement.
- Opted in the whole time. If someone leaves and rejoins, their consecutive count starts again.
- Using the app. Google does not publish a minimum number of opens, but the production form asks how testers engaged and whether usage matched what you expect in production. Testers who install once and disappear are the main reason applications fail.

### A realistic timeline

1. Day 0: create the closed track, add testers (an email list or a Google Group), upload an app bundle and send the release for review.
2. Hours to a few days later: the release is published and the opt-in link works. Google notes the first test link can take several hours to become available.
3. Days 1 to 14: at least 12 testers stay opted in and use the app. Ship at least one update based on their feedback.
4. Day 15 or later: click Apply for production on the Dashboard and answer the questions.
5. About a week later: Google says the review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer. You get an email when it's done.
6. After approval: the Production page unlocks. Your first production release still goes through normal app review.

Plan for roughly three to four weeks from your first closed-test upload to a public listing, if nothing goes wrong.

### The production access form

Google's form has three parts. Part one is about your closed test: how easy it was to recruit testers, how they engaged, and a summary of their feedback and how you collected it. Part two is about your app: target audience, what value it gives users, and how many installs you expect in the first year. Part three is about production readiness: what you changed after the test and how you decided the app was ready.

Write the answers before you open the form. Google warns that your answers are lost if you leave the page before clicking Next or Apply. Our guide to the production access questions and the free answer tool at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ help you draft them from real numbers.

### Why apps don't pass

Google's Help Center lists two reasons you may need to keep running your closed test: fewer than 12 opted-in testers, or not enough engagement from testers. In practice developers hit these problems:

- Asking exactly 12 people. One dropout on day 10 and you are at 11.
- Testers who install and never open the app again.
- Many accounts on one phone, or accounts that are not real people.
- No updates and no feedback during the 14 days, so there is nothing to describe in the form.
- Short, generic answers in the questionnaire.

If you already got a "more testing required" reply, read the guide on insufficient testing engagement and the guide on what to do when production access is rejected.

### Where to get 12 testers

Google does not say where testers must come from. Friends and family work if you know enough Android users who will open your app daily for two weeks. Test-for-test communities are free but need your time. Paid services are faster.

Tester Exchange does both. Pay once ($12.99 for 12 testers, $14.99 for 15, $22.99 for 25), or get testers free by testing other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn in your Android phone's browser. Every tester is a real person on their own phone, and you see daily use for each one. We recommend 15 testers so a dropout or two can't push you under 12.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it 12 or 20 testers?** 12. Google lowered it from 20 to 12 in December 2024. The 14 continuous days stayed the same.

**Does the requirement apply to my old account?** Only personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run the closed test. Older personal accounts and organization accounts are not covered by it.

**Do I need to repeat closed testing for every app?** Production access is granted per app on affected personal accounts, so plan a closed test for each new app.

**Does internal testing count?** No. It has to be a closed test. Google also says people opted into your internal test can't join your closed test until they leave the internal one.

**Do testers have to use the app every day?** Google doesn't publish a minimum. It asks about engagement in the production form, so regular real use by most testers is the safest pattern.

**How long does Google take to review production access?** Google says usually seven days or less, but it can occasionally take longer.

---

## After the 14 days: production access review time and your first release
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/google-play-review-time-after-closed-testing/

Your closed test has had at least 12 testers opted in for 14 days in a row. The Apply for production button is waiting. What happens next, and how long until your app is actually on Google Play? There are two separate waits: Google's review of your production access application, then the normal review of your first production release. This guide walks through both, using Google's Help Center for the official parts.

### Before you click Apply

- At least 12 testers are opted in right now. Google requires this on the day you apply, not just at some point.
- Those testers have been opted in for at least 14 consecutive days.
- Testers actually used the app, and you can describe how.
- You have feedback to summarize and at least one change you made because of it.
- Your App content declarations, store listing and Policy status have no open issues.

Don't close the closed test or remove testers when you apply. If Google wants more testing, you'll need them.

### Applying for production access

1. Open Play Console and go to your app's Dashboard.
2. Click Apply for production. Google shows this once the closed testing requirement is met.
3. Answer the three parts: about your closed test (recruiting, engagement, feedback), about your app (audience, value, expected installs in year one) and about production readiness (what you changed and how you know it's ready).
4. Click Apply. Google warns that answers are lost if you leave the page before Next or Apply, so draft them elsewhere first.

The guide on production access questions explains each question, and the free tool at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ drafts answers from your real numbers.

### How long the review takes

Google's Help Center says the review of a production access application usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer. The account owner gets an email when the review is complete.

Google doesn't publish a way to speed this up. Waiting a few extra days past a week is not unusual, and contacting support usually won't change the timing. Use the time to keep testing and fixing bugs; testers stay on your closed track.

### The two possible outcomes

- Approved: you can access the Production page and publish your app on Google Play. Open testing also becomes available.
- More testing needed: Google says you may need to continue running your closed test, for example if you had fewer than 12 opted-in testers or not enough engagement. See the guide on what to do when production access is rejected.

### Your first production release

Production access is not the same as being live. You still need to create a production release, and it goes through Google's normal app review like any other app. Google doesn't promise a fixed time for this review. New apps from new accounts often take longer than updates from established ones, so allow several days and plan your launch date with margin.

1. Go to Test and release, then Production, then Create new release.
2. Promote the build from your closed track, or upload a new .aab. Using the build your testers already ran is the safer choice.
3. Write release notes and choose countries.
4. Consider a staged rollout (for example 20% of users) so you can catch problems early.
5. Send the changes for review in Publishing overview. If managed publishing is on, click Publish after approval to go live when you choose.
6. Once approved and published, the app can take a little while to appear in Play Store search. Share the direct link in the meantime.

### Full timeline from the first upload

- Closed track setup and first review: hours to a few days.
- Closed test: at least 14 days once 12 testers are opted in.
- Production access review: usually seven days or less, according to Google.
- First production release review: often a few days; can be longer.
- Total: plan on about four weeks from first closed-test upload to public listing, and more if anything needs fixing.

### After launch

Google advises continuing to test your app before publishing production updates. Keep the closed track as a beta channel for your early testers, and consider open testing for a larger audience.

If you haven't reached day 14 yet, the biggest time saver is starting with enough testers. Tester Exchange sends real people on their own Android phones: $12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15 or $22.99 for 25, paid once, or free if you test other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn. We recommend 15 so a dropout can't push you under 12 right before you apply.

### Frequently asked questions

**How long does Google take to approve production access?** Google says the review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer.

**Is my app live once production access is approved?** No. You still create a production release, which goes through normal app review before it's published.

**Can testers leave once I've applied?** Keep them until you're approved. Google requires at least 12 opted-in testers when you apply, and you may need to continue the test.

**Why is the Apply for production button missing?** It appears once you meet the requirement: at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days. Check the Dashboard for your current count.

**Can I speed up the review?** Google doesn't offer a way to. Make sure there are no policy or declaration issues so the review isn't held up.

---

## Rejected after closed testing? How to fix "more testing required"
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/insufficient-testing-engagement/

You ran a closed test with 12 testers for 14 days, applied for production, and Google said your app needs more testing. This is the most common outcome for new personal accounts. It usually means Google didn't see enough real use of your app during the test. Here's what Google looks at, and how to run a second test that passes.

### Why Google says your app needs more testing

Opting in is not the same as testing. Google can see how many testers installed the app, how often they opened it, and whether you shipped updates during the test. A test where people installed once and never came back looks like a box being ticked, not a real test.

- Low engagement: testers installed the app but rarely or never opened it.
- Too few active testers: people left the test, and you dropped below 12 opted-in testers.
- No iteration: no new builds and no visible response to feedback during the 14 days.
- Weak answers: vague replies in the production questionnaire, with no numbers and no examples of feedback.

### A plan that passes on the second try

1. Keep the closed test running. Don't delete the track or remove testers who are still active.
2. Recruit 14–15 real testers who will open the app daily, so a few dropouts don't push you under 12.
3. Give testers one or two concrete tasks per week ("create an account, add an item, change a setting").
4. Ask for written feedback, fix at least a few reported issues, and upload new builds to the closed track during the test.
5. Keep a log: daily active testers, total tester-days, feedback received, and what you changed.
6. After 14 more days of real use, apply again and answer every question with those numbers.

### Show proof of engagement

Your answers should read like a short test report: how many testers, how many days they used the app, what they reported, and which builds fixed it. Tester Exchange records each day every tester opens your app and drafts these answers from that data, so you don't have to reconstruct them from memory.

### What not to do

- Don't use your own spare phones or accounts as testers. Many accounts on one device don't count as real testing.
- Don't pay for "testers" who only install and never open the app. That's exactly what gets rejected.
- Don't copy generic answers from the internet. Use your own numbers and your own feedback.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do I have to restart the 14 days?** You keep your closed test, but Google wants to see more real testing before you apply again. Plan for at least another 14 days of active use.

**How often should testers open the app?** Google doesn't publish a number. Daily use by most testers is the safest pattern, and it's what Tester Exchange records for every tester.

**Does feedback matter?** Yes. The questionnaire asks what testers said and what you changed. Real feedback and real fixes make your answers credible.

---

## How to keep closed testers active for all 14 days
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/keep-testers-active-14-days/

Finding 12 testers is only half the job. Most of them install the app on day one, open it a few times, and then forget it. Google reviews whether testers really used your app, so a quiet second week can sink the whole test. These tactics keep people opening your app until day 14.

### Why engagement matters

There are two hurdles. First, the 14-day clock only counts while at least 12 testers are opted in, so people leaving the test can stall your progress. Second, when you apply for production, Google reviews whether testers actually used the app during the test.

A list of 12 opted-in testers who stopped opening the app after day two meets the first hurdle on paper and fails the second. Engagement is what turns a closed test into a real test.

### Practical tactics that keep testers coming back

1. Recruit 14–15 testers, not 12. Someone always gets busy, changes phones or loses interest. The extra testers are your buffer.
2. Give one concrete task per day. "Open the app" is easy to forget. "Today, create a list and share it" gives a reason to come back. A short checklist for the whole test works too.
3. Push an update mid-test and say what changed. Upload a new build to the closed track around the end of week one and tell testers what's new and what to try.
4. Ask for written feedback. Two or three specific questions get better answers than "any thoughts?". Reply, and fix what you can.
5. Remind on day 3, day 7 and day 12. Day 3 catches people who never really started, day 7 restarts the second week, day 12 gets everyone over the finish line.
6. Replace dropouts quickly. As soon as a tester goes quiet for a couple of days, invite a new one so you stay above 12.

### A simple 14-day plan

- Day 1: welcome message, install link and the task list.
- Day 3: first reminder and a quick check of who hasn't opened the app.
- Days 5–8: upload a new build with fixes and announce what changed.
- Day 7: reminder plus a short feedback question.
- Day 12: final reminder and a request for written feedback.
- Day 14: thank your testers and note your numbers for the production application.

### How Tester Exchange helps

- Daily use recorded: each day a tester opens your app is shown on your app page.
- Daily report: see how many testers were active each day, plus the feedback they sent, so you spot dropouts early.
- Production answers: get draft answers for the production-access questions based on your real test data.

Google still makes the final decision on production access. These tools help you run a test that reflects real use and explain it clearly.

### Frequently asked questions

**My testers stopped opening the app. What should I do?** Message them with one specific task, push a small update so there's something new to try, and invite replacements right away for anyone who doesn't come back.

**How often should testers open the app?** Google doesn't publish a number. Regular use by most testers across all 14 days is the safest pattern, and daily use is the clearest signal.

**What happens if I drop below 12 testers?** The 14 days only count while at least 12 testers are opted in. Recruit 14–15 so a few dropouts don't stall your progress.

**Should I really release an update during the test?** Yes. A new build that fixes reported issues shows Google that you used the test to improve the app, and it gives testers a reason to open it again.

**Is written feedback required?** The production questionnaire asks what testers told you and what you changed. Written feedback gives you real examples to point to.

---

## Organization vs personal Google Play developer account
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/organization-vs-personal-developer-account/

The 12 testers, 14 days rule applies to personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023. Organization accounts are not covered by it. That makes many solo developers ask whether they should register as a business instead. Sometimes that's the right call, but an organization account needs a real legal entity, a D-U-N-S number and a verified website. This guide compares both, using Google's Help Center as the source.

### The two account types

- Personal: Google describes it as meant for personal use, such as students, hobbyists and amateur developers. You verify your own legal name and address.
- Organization: for businesses and organizations, including commercial, professional and government activity. You verify the organization with a D-U-N-S number, an official phone number and an organization website.

Google says both account types have the same core functionality. Both can sell apps and in-app products once a payments profile is set up.

### The testing difference

Google requires personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days, then apply for production access. Organization accounts don't have this step: they can release to production once the app passes normal review.

That saves about three weeks per app. But it is the only real advantage for most indie developers, and getting an organization account can take longer than three weeks if you don't already have a company and a D-U-N-S number.

### When an organization account is required

Google says some kinds of apps must be published from an organization account. These include:

- Financial products and services, such as banking, loans, stock trading and crypto wallets or exchanges.
- Health apps, such as medical apps and human subjects research apps.
- Apps approved to use Android's VpnService class.
- Government apps, made by or for a government agency.

If your app is in one of these categories, you need an organization account regardless of testing.

### What an organization account needs

- A D-U-N-S number for your legal entity from Dun & Bradstreet. Google says you can't create an organization account without a valid one. Applying is free; Google warns about third-party services that charge high fees for it. It can take days to weeks to arrive.
- A legal entity whose name and address match the D-U-N-S record and your Google payments profile.
- An organization website that you verify in Play Console.
- An official organization phone number, plus contact and public developer email addresses and phone numbers, each verified with a one-time code.
- The one-time registration fee that every new developer account pays.

### Converting a personal account

Google's Help Center describes a way to change a personal account into an organization account. In outline:

1. Make sure your personal account is fully verified, with no pending warnings on the Play Console home page.
2. Go to Manage account, then Account details, then About you, and verify your organization's website.
3. Click Change account type and choose or create an organization payments profile with your D-U-N-S number.
4. Enter organization details and contacts, and verify each email and phone.
5. Complete any identity verification Google asks for, then link the payments profile and save.

Google says you can't change an organization account back to personal, and that you should wait at least 72 hours after switching before submitting new apps. Google's page on converting doesn't spell out how apps already in closed testing are treated, so check your Dashboard after the switch before you stop a running test.

### Trade-offs

- Cost: forming a company can mean registration fees, an accountant and yearly filings, depending on your country. Twelve testers cost far less.
- Time: D-U-N-S plus website verification plus organization checks can take longer than a 14-day test.
- Credibility: a company name can look more trustworthy to users and partners.
- No way back: you can't convert an organization account to personal.

### Which should you choose?

1. Your app is finance, health, VPN or government: organization account.
2. You already have a company with a D-U-N-S number: organization account. It skips the test.
3. You're a solo developer or hobbyist without a company: stay personal and run the closed test. It's faster and cheaper than forming a company only to skip it.
4. You plan many apps and a business anyway: start the company and D-U-N-S process, and run closed tests on your personal account while you wait.

### If you stay personal

You need at least 12 real testers for 14 days, and we recommend 15. Tester Exchange sends real people on their own Android phones: $12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15, or $22.99 for 25 testers, paid once. Or get testers free by testing other developers' apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do organization accounts need 12 testers?** No. The closed testing requirement applies to personal accounts created after 13 November 2023.

**Can I get a D-U-N-S number as an individual?** D-U-N-S numbers are issued to business entities. Sole proprietorships can be registered in some countries; check with Dun & Bradstreet for yours. Applying is free.

**Can I switch from personal to organization?** Yes. Google describes a Change account type option under Manage account, Account details. It needs a verified organization website and a D-U-N-S number.

**Can I switch back to personal later?** No. Google says organization accounts can't be changed to personal. You would need a new account and an app transfer.

**Is an organization account worth it just to skip testing?** Usually not for a solo developer. Forming a company and getting verified often costs more time and money than a 14-day closed test.

---

## What to check before you pay for Google Play closed testers
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/paid-closed-testers-checklist/

If your personal Google Play developer account was created after 13 November 2023, you need a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before you can apply for production access. Many developers pay someone to supply those testers. Paying is fine, but the test only helps you if the testers are real and stay opted in. Use this checklist before you hand over money.

### What Google actually requires

Google's Play Console Help states that personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run a closed test with a minimum of 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days. When you meet this, you can apply for production access from the Dashboard and answer questions about your app, your testing and your readiness.

Nothing in that rule is about how you found the testers. What matters is that the opt-ins are real and continuous, and that your answers describe a test you really ran.

### Seven things to check before you buy

1. Real people on real phones. Ask whether each tester uses their own Android device. Emulators and shared devices make for a weak test and a weak production answer.
2. More than 12. The 14 days only count while at least 12 testers stay opted in. A service that gives you exactly 12 leaves no room for one person to leave. Ask for 14 or 15.
3. Continuous opt-in. Google's rule says continuously. Ask how the service keeps testers opted in for the full period.
4. Proof of daily use. You should be able to see, day by day, that the app was opened. If you can't see it, you can't describe it in the production questions.
5. Replacements for dropouts. Ask what happens when a tester leaves on day 6. A good answer is a replacement, not silence.
6. Your account, your control. You add testers through your own Google Group or email list. Never share your Play Console login.
7. Honest wording. No one can promise Google's decision. Be cautious of guarantees of production access.

### After you pay: keep the test honest

Open the app yourself, read the feedback testers send, and ship at least one update that fixes something they reported. The production questions ask what testers told you and what you changed, so real answers are easy to write when the test was real.

### How Tester Exchange works

- Real testers: people with their own Android phones install your app from your closed test.
- Daily use recorded: each day a tester opens your app is logged, and seats a tester stops using go to a new tester.
- Daily report: see how many testers were active, plus their feedback.

Google makes the final decision on production access. This gives you a test that reflects real use and the data to explain it.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is it allowed to pay for closed testers?** Google's requirement is 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days. The help page does not say how you must find them, but the test should reflect real use of your app.

**How many testers should I get?** Get 14 or 15. The 14 days only count while at least 12 testers are opted in.

**Do testers need to open the app every day?** Google doesn't publish a number. Regular use across all 14 days is the safest pattern.

**Can anyone guarantee production access?** No. Google decides. Treat any guarantee with caution.

**Do organization accounts need this?** The requirement applies to personal accounts created after 13 November 2023, according to Google's help page.

---

## How to answer Google Play's production access questions
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/production-access-questions/

When your closed test is done, Play Console asks you to apply for production and fill in a short questionnaire. Your answers, together with the test data Google can see, decide whether you get access. Good answers are specific: real numbers, real feedback and real changes.

### Questions about your closed test

- How easy was it to recruit testers? Play Console asks you to pick an option here, not to write text. Choose the one that honestly fits: Google can see how your test went.
- Describe the engagement you received. Give numbers: how many testers installed, how many stayed opted in for 14 days in a row, and how long the test ran. Also say whether testers used all the features, and whether their use matched how real users will use the app, including any differences.
- Summarize the feedback. Name two or three concrete themes ("sign-up was confusing", "crash when rotating the screen") and say how you collected it.

### Questions about your app

- Who is the intended audience? Be specific: who they are and what problem they have.
- How does your app provide value? One or two sentences on what users can do that they couldn't before.
- How many installs do you expect in the first year? Pick an honest range. Nobody expects a big number from a new developer.

### Questions about production readiness

- What changes did you make based on the test? List the fixes and improvements, and mention the builds you uploaded during the test.
- How did you decide your app is ready? Use criteria: key flows work, reported crashes are fixed, testers used it for the full period.

### Example answer (engagement)

"14 testers installed the app from the closed track and used it over 15 days. On average 12 testers were active each day, for 186 tester-days in total, with around 4 minutes per session. We sent testers a short task list each week and asked them to report anything confusing. 13 testers completed the full period."

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I answer in my own language?** Yes, but clear, simple English is safest, because reviewers may not read your language.

**How long are the answers?** Two to five sentences each is enough. Specific beats long.

**What if I don't have numbers?** Then you probably need more testing. Track daily active testers and feedback before you apply.

---

## Production access rejected: what to do next
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/production-access-rejected/

You ran your closed test, applied for production, waited about a week, and Google said no. It feels like starting over, but usually it isn't. In most cases your closed track, your testers and your app all stay in place, and Google simply wants to see more or better testing before it lets the app go public. This guide explains what the decision means and gives you a plan for the next application.

### What a rejection means

Google's Help Center says you may need to keep running your closed test before getting production access. The reasons it lists include having fewer than 12 opted-in testers and testers not being engaged enough with your app during the test.

So a rejection is usually not a policy strike against your account. It's Google saying the evidence from your test wasn't convincing yet. Read the email and the message in Play Console carefully: it usually points at testing, engagement or the answers you gave.

- "More testing required" or similar: keep the closed test running and collect more real use.
- Fewer than 12 opted-in testers: some testers left. Recruit more before applying again.
- Policy or content problems: a separate issue. Check the Policy status page and fix those first, or a new application won't help.

### First, don't do these

- Don't delete the closed track or remove testers who are still active. You need them.
- Don't create a new app with a new package name to "start fresh". You would have to run a whole new closed test anyway.
- Don't apply again the next day with the same answers. Nothing has changed, so expect the same outcome.
- Don't fill seats with your own spare phones or fake accounts. Google can see when many accounts share one device.

### Find the weak spot

Open your closed track in Play Console and the statistics for the test period. Ask yourself honestly:

- How many testers were still opted in on the day you applied? Was it comfortably over 12?
- How many of them opened the app on most days, not just on day one?
- Did you upload at least one new build during the test?
- Can you quote real feedback from testers and name what you changed because of it?
- Did your answers in the form include numbers, or were they a sentence or two of general text?

Most rejected applications fail on engagement and on vague answers. Both are fixable in two weeks.

### A plan for the next application

1. Fix any policy issues first, if the email mentioned them.
2. Check your tester count. Recruit until you have 15 or more real testers opted in, so dropouts can't take you under 12.
3. Give testers concrete tasks each week, such as "sign up, create your first item, try the settings screen". Vague requests produce vague use.
4. Collect written feedback with a simple form or email address, and keep a log.
5. Fix several reported issues and upload new builds to the closed track during the test.
6. Run the test for at least another 14 days with real daily use. Google doesn't publish a fixed waiting period, so let the evidence build up rather than watching the calendar.
7. Rewrite your answers with numbers: testers opted in, how many used the app regularly, tester-days, bugs found and fixed, builds shipped.
8. Apply again from the Dashboard. Google says review usually takes seven days or less.

### Write better answers

Google's form asks how easy recruiting was, how testers engaged, what feedback you got and how you collected it, who the app is for, its value, expected installs, what you changed after testing and how you know it's ready.

Treat it like a short test report. "15 testers, 13 used the app on at least 10 of 14 days, 21 feedback messages, 3 crashes fixed in builds 1.0.2 and 1.0.3, onboarding shortened from 4 screens to 2" is far stronger than "testers liked the app". Our free tool at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ turns your numbers into draft answers, and the guide on production access questions covers each question.

### If your testers were the problem

If most of your first testers installed once and disappeared, a second round with the same people will look the same. Replace them with people who will open the app daily.

Tester Exchange sends real people who use your app on their own Android phones and shows daily use for each tester, so you can see engagement while the test runs rather than finding out from a rejection. You can pay once ($12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15, $22.99 for 25 testers) or earn testers free by testing other apps at https://testerexchange.com/earn. If a tester stops, a new one takes the seat.

### Frequently asked questions

**Do I have to restart the 14 days from zero?** Google says you may need to continue running your closed test. Keep the existing track and testers, and plan for at least another two weeks of real use before reapplying.

**How long must I wait before reapplying?** Google's Help Center doesn't state a fixed waiting period. Apply again when you have clearly more and better testing to show.

**Will a rejection hurt my developer account?** A production access decision about testing is not the same as a policy violation. Policy problems are shown separately on the Policy status page.

**Can I appeal instead?** For a testing decision, the practical route is more testing and a stronger application. For policy enforcement, follow the appeal link in that specific email.

**Should I switch to an organization account?** Only if you are a real business with a D-U-N-S number. Organization accounts aren't subject to the closed testing requirement, but converting takes verification and time. See the guide on organization vs personal accounts.

## Reddit tester swaps vs Tester Exchange
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/reddit-vs-tester-exchange/

Reddit is a good free place to find other developers who need to test too. Communities such as r/AndroidClosedTesting and r/TestersCommunity are full of "I test yours, you test mine" posts. It works when both sides keep their promise for 14 days. The difficulty is tracking that by hand.

### How Reddit swaps work

- You post that you need testers for your app and offer to test someone else's.
- You collect emails or a Google Group, add them to your closed test, and test their apps in return.
- You track every tester's days yourself, with a spreadsheet or by asking.

### What goes wrong

- Testers install and forget. You find out after you apply.
- Dropouts. People leave on day 4 to 7, and you drop under 12 without noticing.
- No proof. You have no per-day record to use in your answers.
- Time. Writing posts, replying and testing many apps every day adds up.

### Reddit versus Tester Exchange

- Price. Reddit is free. Tester Exchange is free if you test other apps, or $12.99 for 12 and $14.99 for 15 testers if you pay.
- Tracking. Tester Exchange counts a day when the tester opens your app on their own phone, and shows it per tester.
- Fairness. Credits keep effort even: you earn by testing, and unused credits stay in your account.
- Reach. Reddit has far more people than any one service. Use both: ask on Reddit, and let Tester Exchange track the days.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Reddit enough to get 12 testers?** It can be, if you recruit more than 12 and follow up daily. Many developers use Reddit plus a tracker.

**Can I post my Tester Exchange link on Reddit?** Read each community's rules first. Many allow test swaps and restrict ads or repeated promotion.

**Does Tester Exchange work with testers I find myself?** Yes. Share your app's page with friends, family or Reddit users, and Tester Exchange checks each person's daily use.

**Which is better?** Reddit is free and broad; Tester Exchange saves tracking time. Combining them is the most reliable route.

## Tester Exchange referral program
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/referral-program/

Short answer: share your personal link. When a friend signs up through it and their phone logs a first verified day of testing, you both receive credits. Credits pay for testers on your own app. This page describes the program as it runs today.

### How it works

1. Sign in to Tester Exchange and open the invite card to copy your personal link. It is the site address with ?ref= and your code at the end.
2. A friend opens your link and signs up. The link is remembered until they sign in.
3. They become a tester and their phone logs a first verified day of use. A verified day needs the companion app and real foreground use of a tested app.
4. At that moment both of you receive credits automatically. There is nothing to claim.

### What you receive

- You (the inviter): 30 credits for each friend whose first verified day is logged.
- Your friend: 15 credits.
- Credits are used to buy tester seats on your own app. One tester seat costs 15 credits (14 tester-days plus a 1-credit feedback budget), so one invite covers two testers' worth of credits.

These amounts are the current settings and can change; the invite card in the app always shows today's numbers.

### The rules

- A new account can attach an inviter once, within 14 days of signing up.
- You cannot invite yourself, and two people cannot be each other's inviter.
- Rewards are limited to 50 rewarded invites per person.
- The reward is paid once per invited person, on their first verified day. Phones are registered, so one phone cannot earn for two accounts.
- Credits are for use inside Tester Exchange. They are not cash and do not convert back to money.

### What this program is not

This is a one-time credit reward for each real new tester. It is not a recurring commission on purchases and there is no cash payout for referrals at the moment.

### Frequently asked questions

**Where do I find my referral link?** Sign in at https://testerexchange.com/ and open the invite card; your link is shown there with a copy button.

**When are credits paid?** Automatically, when the invited person's phone logs their first verified day of testing.

**Is there a limit?** Yes: 50 rewarded invites per person, and a new account can attach an inviter only within 14 days of signing up.

**Can I withdraw referral credits as cash?** No. Credits are used inside Tester Exchange to buy tester seats.

## Rejected with "more testing required"? Here is how to fix it
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/rejected-more-testing-required/

If Google rejected your production access application and said you need to keep testing, your app is usually not banned. Google is saying your test did not show enough real use or enough detail. The fix is almost always the same: keep the closed test running, show real daily use by at least 12 opted-in testers, and rewrite your answers with numbers. This page gives you the plan and sample answers to adapt.

### Why Google says "more testing required"

Google's Help Center says you may need to continue your closed test before you can get production access, and lists causes such as fewer than 12 opted-in testers or testers who were not engaged enough with the app (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465). Google does not publish the exact check it runs.

- Testers installed once and never came back. The most common reason people report.
- Dropouts took you under 12. Count again on the day you applied, not on day one.
- Thin answers. One or two general sentences per question, with no numbers or changes you made.

### The 2-week fix plan

1. Keep your closed track and active testers. Do not delete the track or start a new app.
2. Recruit up to 15 or more testers so a dropout cannot take you under 12.
3. Ask every tester to open the app on their own phone every day for 14 days. Ask for one short written note per week.
4. Upload at least one new build during the run and write down what changed and why.
5. On day 10, collect your numbers: testers opted in, tester-days of real use, feedback received, bugs fixed, builds shipped.
6. Apply on day 15 or later, with answers built from those numbers.

### Sample answers to adapt

These examples use made-up numbers to show the level of detail Google's questions need. Replace every number and detail with your own, and never claim anything that did not happen.

How easy was it to recruit testers? Pick the option that is honestly true. Google asks you to choose, not to write text.

Describe the engagement you received from testers. Example: "15 testers were opted in on the day we applied. 13 opened the app on at least 10 of the 14 days. Most sessions were 2 to 5 minutes. Testers used the main flow (sign up, create an item, share it) and the settings screen."

Summarize the feedback you received. Example: "We received 21 written messages. The top three issues were a crash when rotating the phone, a confusing second onboarding screen, and slow loading on mobile data."

What changes did you make based on testing? Example: "We fixed the rotation crash in build 1.0.2, cut onboarding from 4 screens to 2 in build 1.0.3, and cached the first list so it loads in about 1 second."

How do you know the app is ready for production? Example: "No crashes were reported in the last 7 days, all high-priority issues are closed, and 13 of 15 testers kept using the app until the end of the test."

Our free generator at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/ turns your own numbers into draft answers. Always edit the draft so it matches what actually happened.

### If your testers were the problem

If your first testers installed and disappeared, a second round with the same people will look the same. Tester Exchange sends real people who use your app on their own Android phones, shows daily use per tester, and replaces any tester who stops. The test run is planned as 16 days: Google's 14 days plus 2 buffer days, with a day 0 to 16 timeline in your dashboard.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does "more testing required" mean my app is banned?** No. Google says you may need to keep running your closed test. Keep your track and active testers, improve the evidence, and apply again.

**Do I have to restart the 14 days from zero?** Google does not say you must start from zero, but you should plan for at least another 14 days of real daily use with 12 or more opted-in testers before reapplying.

**How long should I wait before applying again?** Google does not publish a fixed waiting period. Let the evidence build for about two weeks, then apply when you have numbers to show.

**Will a tester service guarantee approval?** No service can guarantee approval, because Google makes the decision. A good service gives you real daily use and records you can use in your answers.

**Can I copy the sample answers?** Only as a format. Use your own real numbers and facts. Answers that do not match your test data can hurt your application.

## How to set up a closed testing track in Play Console, step by step
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/set-up-closed-testing-track/

Before your 14-day clock can start, you need a closed testing track that is published, has testers attached, and gives you an opt-in link that works. Most problems later on, such as testers seeing "app not available", come from a step missed here. This guide follows the current Play Console menus (Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing) and Google's Help Center.

### Before you start

- A Play Console developer account with identity verification finished.
- Your app created in Play Console, with the store listing, content rating, target audience, data safety and other App content declarations filled in. Play Console won't let you send a release for review while required items are missing.
- A signed Android App Bundle (.aab) with a package name you are happy to keep forever. You can't change it later.
- A plan for your testers: at least 12, ideally 15, real people with Android phones and Google Accounts.

### 1. Open or create the closed track

1. In Play Console, pick your app.
2. Go to Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing.
3. Play Console gives you a default closed track (often called Alpha). Use it. You can create extra closed tracks, but one is all you need for the requirement.
4. Click Manage track.

### 2. Choose countries and regions

Open the Countries / regions tab and add the countries where your testers live. A tester in a country you didn't select will not be able to install the app.

Google notes that changes to distributed countries apply across tracks, and that additional closed tracks don't support their own country targeting. If your testers are spread around the world, the simplest choice is to add every country you can legally ship to.

### 3. Add testers: email list or Google Group

Open the Testers tab. You have two options, and you can use both on one track.

- Email list: click Create email list, name it, then type addresses or upload a CSV. Google allows up to 2,000 users per list. Uploading a CSV overwrites the addresses already in that list. Every address must be the Google Account the tester uses on their phone's Play Store.
- Google Group: enter the group's address, such as yourgroup@googlegroups.com. Only members of the group can join your test, and they must join the group before they opt in. Adding someone to the group is all you do; you don't touch Play Console again.

If you use Tester Exchange, add the group testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com under Google Groups and save. That one address lets every tester we send install your app. See also the guide on Google Group vs email list.

### 4. Add a feedback channel

On the same Testers tab, add a feedback URL or an email address. Testers see it when they join. You will need to summarize tester feedback in the production access form, so make it easy: a short Google Form or a dedicated email address works.

### 5. Create the release and send it for review

1. On the closed track, click Create new release.
2. Upload your .aab. Let Play App Signing manage your key unless you have a reason not to.
3. Add a release name and short release notes, for example "First closed test build".
4. Click Next, fix any errors, then Save.
5. Go to Publishing overview and send the changes for review. If managed publishing is on, you also have to click Publish after approval.

Closed test releases on new accounts are reviewed before they go live. Times vary from hours to several days.

### 6. Share the opt-in link

Google says the opt-in link appears only once the app status is Published. Copy it from the Testers tab. It looks like https://play.google.com/apps/testing/your.package.name.

The first time you publish, the link can take several hours to start working. Testers can't find closed tests by searching Google Play, so they need either this link or the Play Store link to your app.

1. The tester signs in to the same Google Account you added (or that is in your Google Group).
2. They open the opt-in link and tap to become a tester.
3. They install your app from Google Play using the link on that page.
4. They open it, and keep opening it during the 14 days.

### 7. Check that the 14 days are counting

Your Dashboard shows the closed testing requirement and how many testers are opted in. Check it every couple of days. If the number falls under 12, recruit replacements straight away, because the requirement counts 12 testers opted in continuously.

During the test, upload at least one new build to the same track. It shows Google you acted on feedback, and testers on the track get the update automatically.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I use internal testing instead?** No. The requirement needs a closed test. Google also says people opted into your internal test can't join a closed test until they leave the internal one.

**Should I use an email list or a Google Group?** A Google Group is easier when testers come and go, because you never edit the track. An email list is fine for a fixed group of friends. You can use both.

**Why don't I see the opt-in link?** It only shows once the release on the closed track is published. Check Publishing overview for pending review or changes not yet sent.

**Does a tester need a Google Account?** Yes. Google says users need a Google Account or Google Workspace account to join a test, and it must be the account on their phone's Play Store.

**Can I make the closed test app paid?** You can, but Google says testers must buy paid apps in closed tests. Keep the test app free to avoid losing testers.

---

## Test for test: how to get 12 closed-test testers without paying
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/test-for-test-closed-testing/

"Test for test" is the most common way solo developers pass Google Play's closed-testing rule: you install and use other developers' apps, and they do the same for yours. It works when every tester really opens the app for 14 days in a row. This guide explains what makes test-for-test succeed or fail, and how Tester Exchange tracks the days for you.

### The rule you are solving

Google's Play Console Help says personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run a closed test with at least 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days before applying for production access (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465).

Test for test is simply two developers meeting that rule for each other.

### Why informal test-for-test often fails

- Nobody tracks the days. In a chat group you only find out on day 12 that a tester opted out on day 5.
- Testers join and vanish. When one leaves, you are back under 12.
- Uneven effort. You test five apps, and two of them never open yours.
- Too few spare testers. Exactly 12 leaves no room for one drop-out.

### How Tester Exchange makes it fair

- Credits keep it even. You earn 1 credit for each day you open an app for at least 30 seconds; one tester costs 15 credits, so 12 testers cost 180.
- Days are counted for you. A tester is paid only for the days they open your app, and unused credits return to your balance.
- Owners who test go first. Apps whose owners opened at least 3 other apps today or yesterday get testers before apps whose owners do not.
- Ask for 14–15 testers, not 12, so one drop-out does not stop your test.

### Step by step

1. Set up your closed test in Play Console and keep the opt-in link handy.
2. On your Android phone, open https://testerexchange.com/earn and sign in with the Google Account your Play Store uses.
3. Join the first app's test, install it from Google Play and open it for 30 seconds. Repeat for the next apps.
4. Add your own app and share its page with anyone who might help.
5. Test a little every day. After 14 days with 12 or more testers opted in, apply for production access.

### Fair-play rules

- Your own real phone. No emulators, cloud phones or device farms.
- One account per person.
- Stay for the full 14 days. Leaving early hurts the developer the same way it would hurt you.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is test for test allowed?** Google's rule is about having at least 12 opted-in testers for 14 days; it does not say where the testers come from. Use real people on real phones.

**How many credits do I need?** 180 credits for 12 testers (15 each). Asking for 15 testers needs 225.

**Do I have to pay?** No. You pay with about a minute a day per app you test. Paying is optional and only makes it faster.

**Do I need an Android phone?** Yes. These are Google Play closed tests, tested on an Android phone signed in to the account your Play Store uses.

---

## Testers Community vs Tester Exchange
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/testers-community-vs-tester-exchange/

Both services help you meet Google Play's closed-testing rule: 12 testers opted in for at least 14 days in a row. Testers Community is the more established service: its website says it has run Google Play closed tests since February 2024. Tester Exchange is newer. This page compares how they work so you can choose. "Tester exchange" is also a plain phrase for swapping tests; Tester Exchange here means our service at testerexchange.com. Competitor details on this page come from their public listings and websites as we read them in October and November 2026 (figures re-checked on 24 November 2026), and may have changed. Check their current pages before you decide.

### The short version

- Testers Community is a free app on Google Play built around a credit exchange: you test other people's apps and earn credits for testers on yours. It also sells managed testers, and its Google Play listing shows 50K+ downloads as of 24 Nov 2026.
- Tester Exchange works the same way (earn credits by testing, or pay once), and checks each tester's daily use on the phone before credits are paid. It is newer and has fewer users, so expect fewer apps and testers on the platform.
- If you do not mind spending time every day in an exchange, either can cost you nothing. If your time matters more, the paid options on both save hours.

### Side by side

- Model. Testers Community: free credit exchange plus paid managed testers. Tester Exchange: free credit exchange plus paid testers.
- Size. Testers Community: its Google Play listing shows 50K+ downloads and a 4.7 rating from about 2.5K ratings (as of 24 Nov 2026), and its website says 50,000+ apps have been published through its free community app (its own figure, not independently verified). Tester Exchange: new and small.
- Paid price (as listed). Testers Community lists $15 for 15 testers and $25 for 25 on its website (as of 24 Nov 2026). Tester Exchange lists $12.99 for 12, $14.99 for 15 and $24.99 for 25 in US dollars, with lower fixed prices in some countries. Prices change, so check both sites.
- Time cost in the free exchange. Both ask you to test other developers' apps. In any credit exchange, 12 testers for 14 days means testing roughly 12 other apps for 14 days, which is real daily work.
- Proof of use. Tester Exchange counts a day only when the tester opened your app on their own phone, and shows each tester's days in your dashboard. Testers Community has its own checks, which we do not describe because we cannot see inside them.
- Production answers. Testers Community says its paid plans include pre-filled answers for Google's production access form. Tester Exchange has a free answer generator at https://testerexchange.com/tools/production-answers/.
- Test run. Tester Exchange plans a 16-day run (14 required days plus 2 buffer days) and shows a day 0 to 16 timeline in your dashboard.

### Which should you choose?

- Choose Testers Community if you want the more established pool, are fine with a daily routine, and want the free route on the best-known platform.
- Choose Tester Exchange if you want each day verified and visible per tester, a clear day-by-day timeline, and a free replacement if a tester stops.
- Use both. Nothing stops you from asking friends and other exchanges to join your test too. Just keep 15 or more testers opted in so dropouts cannot take you under 12.

### The rule both are solving

Google's Help Center says personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before applying for production access (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465). Neither service can promise approval, because Google makes the decision.

### Frequently asked questions

**Is Testers Community better than Tester Exchange?** It is more established and reports more users. Tester Exchange is newer and smaller and focuses on verifying each tester's daily use and on a clear 16-day timeline. The better fit depends on whether you value pool size or daily proof and a guided run.

**Is Tester Exchange the same as Testers Community?** No. They are separate services run by different people. "Tester exchange" is also a general phrase for swapping tests.

**Are both free?** Both have a free credit exchange where you earn credits by testing other apps, and both sell paid testers. The free route costs your time every day.

**Can I use both at once?** Yes. Your closed test can include testers from several sources, as long as at least 12 stay opted in for 14 days in a row.

**Will either guarantee production access?** No. Google decides. Real daily use and good answers improve your chances.

## TWA app for closed testing: how to switch to a WebView or Capacitor shell
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/twa-app-closed-testing-webview-fix/

Short answer: Google Play accepts a Trusted Web Activity (TWA) like any app, so the 12-tester rule is the same. But some tester services will not take TWA apps, and daily use of one can be hard to measure per app. If that is your case, moving to a Capacitor (WebView) shell is a small change. This guide explains the difference and the steps.

### TWA vs WebView, in plain terms

Neither is better for users on its own. The difference matters for testing because services that record daily use per app read what is in the foreground, and with a TWA the screen belongs to Chrome. We have not verified that Tester Exchange records TWA use reliably, so we recommend a WebView or Capacitor shell for the test.

- TWA: Chrome draws your site full screen. Your app is a thin launcher. It is what PWABuilder and Bubblewrap produce, and it needs Digital Asset Links to hide the address bar.
- WebView / Capacitor: your app draws the screen itself and shows your web content inside it. You can add native features and your app is the one in the foreground.

### Switch from TWA to a Capacitor shell

1. Keep your site. Nothing about your website changes.
2. Keep the same application ID if the TWA is already on a closed track, so you do not restart the count; otherwise start the new app with the ID you will keep.
3. Add Capacitor: npx cap init, npm i @capacitor/android, npx cap add android. Point server.url at your live HTTPS site, or bundle your build folder as webDir.
4. Raise the version code above the TWA release, build a signed .aab in Android Studio and upload it as a new release on the same closed track.
5. Testers who are already opted in keep their opt-in; they receive the update from Google Play.

### Run the closed test: 12 testers for 14 days

Google requires personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row before they can apply for production access. The requirement is the same whatever tool built TWA or WebView app.

1. In Play Console, create the app (name, default language, app or game, free or paid) and fill in the declarations Google asks for.
2. Open Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing. Create a release and upload your signed .aab file.
3. Under Testers, add an email list or a Google Group. If you use Tester Exchange, the group to add is testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com and we add our testers to it.
4. Check Countries / regions includes the countries your testers live in.
5. Send the release for review. When the app status is Published, share the opt-in link; each tester must open it and accept.
6. Keep at least 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days. Aim for 15 so one dropout does not move your date.
7. When the Dashboard shows the Apply for production button, apply and answer the three parts of the form.

No friends with Android phones? Tester Exchange gives you real people on their own phones, each day they open your app is recorded, and dropouts are replaced. You can also test other developers' apps free at https://testerexchange.com/earn and each app you test brings a tester to yours.

### Common mistakes

- Do not create a new application ID just to change shells; that restarts everything.
- Do not remove testers from the track while you switch.
- Do not skip a real-device test: a WebView app can behave differently from Chrome (for example with sign-in pop-ups).
- Keep the Digital Asset Links file in place only if you still ship a TWA.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does Google Play accept TWA apps for closed testing?** Yes. Google treats a TWA as an ordinary app. The 12-tester, 14-day closed test is the same.

**Will switching shells restart my 14 days?** If you upload a new release to the same app and track, testers stay opted in. Creating a new app with a new application ID starts a new test.

**Do I have to give up my PWA?** No. The website stays. Only the Android shell changes.

---

## Website to Android app: publish on Google Play with 12 testers
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/website-to-android-app-12-testers/

Short answer: you can put a website on Google Play, but you still build a signed Android App Bundle and your new personal account still needs a closed test with 12 testers opted in for 14 days. This guide covers the two common approaches and the closed test.

### Two ways to wrap a website

Your site should work well on a phone first: responsive layout, fast loading, HTTPS, and a clear purpose. Google can reject apps that only repackage a website without added value, so give the app something useful of its own.

- WebView or Capacitor: a native Android app loads your site (or a bundled copy) inside its own window. You can add native features. This is the route we recommend.
- Trusted Web Activity (TWA): Chrome shows your site full screen under your app name and you prove ownership with Digital Asset Links. Tools like PWABuilder generate one. See our TWA guide for the trade-offs.

### Build the Capacitor route

1. Make sure your site builds to a folder of static files, or point Capacitor at your live HTTPS URL for a hosted site.
2. Install Node.js and Android Studio.
3. Choose an application ID like com.yourname.yourapp. It cannot change after upload.
4. Run npx cap add android, then npx cap sync android, then npx cap open android.
5. Create a signing key and build a signed Android App Bundle in Android Studio. Test it on a real phone.

### Run the closed test: 12 testers for 14 days

Google requires personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 to run a closed test with at least 12 testers who stay opted in for 14 days in a row before they can apply for production access. The requirement is the same whatever tool built website app.

1. In Play Console, create the app (name, default language, app or game, free or paid) and fill in the declarations Google asks for.
2. Open Test and release, then Testing, then Closed testing. Create a release and upload your signed .aab file.
3. Under Testers, add an email list or a Google Group. If you use Tester Exchange, the group to add is testerexchange-testers@googlegroups.com and we add our testers to it.
4. Check Countries / regions includes the countries your testers live in.
5. Send the release for review. When the app status is Published, share the opt-in link; each tester must open it and accept.
6. Keep at least 12 testers opted in for 14 consecutive days. Aim for 15 so one dropout does not move your date.
7. When the Dashboard shows the Apply for production button, apply and answer the three parts of the form.

No friends with Android phones? Tester Exchange gives you real people on their own phones, each day they open your app is recorded, and dropouts are replaced. You can also test other developers' apps free at https://testerexchange.com/earn and each app you test brings a tester to yours.

### Common mistakes

- Do not upload an app that only shows a "this site is down" or blank screen when offline; add a friendly offline state.
- Do not change the application ID after upload.
- Do not rely on a TWA if you want daily use measured per app; see the TWA guide.
- Aim for 15 testers so a dropout does not move your date.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I just submit my website URL to Google Play?** No. Google Play takes a signed Android App Bundle. A wrapper such as Capacitor or a Trusted Web Activity packages your site into one.

**Is a website wrapper allowed?** Google reviews every app against its developer policies, which include expectations about functionality and user experience. An app that adds nothing beyond a website is at risk, so add real value and read the policy pages for your case.

**Do I need a new Play Console account for an AI-built app?** No. Google Play does not care which tool wrote the code. What matters is the account type: personal accounts created after 13 November 2023 need the 12-tester, 14-day closed test; organization accounts are not subject to that requirement.

**Can the testers be the same for several apps?** Testers opt in per app. A person can test several of your apps, but each person has to opt in to each app separately.

---

## When can I apply for production access on Google Play?
URL: https://testerexchange.com/guide/when-can-i-apply-for-production-access/

Short answer: you can apply once at least 12 testers have each been opted in to your closed test for 14 days in a row and are still opted in. Count 14 days from the day your 12th tester joined, not from the day you published the test. Then Google's review usually takes seven days or less. This page is a day-by-day timeline from Google Play Console Help, with the mistakes that push the date back.

### The rule in one paragraph

Google Play Console Help says personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023 must run a closed test with a minimum of 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days before they can apply for production. When you meet the criteria, the Apply for production button appears on the Dashboard in Play Console.

The clock is per tester. Your earliest apply date is the day the 12th tester completes 14 consecutive opted-in days.

### Day-by-day timeline

1. Day 0: upload a build to a closed testing track and publish the release. Add testers through a Google Group or an email list.
2. Day 0 to 2: testers accept the invite and opt in on the opt-in page, then install the app. Each person's 14 days start when they opt in, so slow joiners move your date back.
3. Day 3 to 13: keep all 12 opted in and using the app. Check the opted-in count every two or three days and replace anyone who leaves at once.
4. Day 14 after the last of your 12 testers joined: every one of the 12 has now been opted in for 14 consecutive days. This is your earliest apply date.
5. Apply day: open the Dashboard, click Apply for production and fill in the three parts: About your closed test, About your app/game, and About your production readiness. Summarize the tester feedback you collected and how you collected it.
6. After applying: Google says review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer. If Google decides the app needs more testing, keep the closed test running and fix the cause.

### Worked example

You publish the closed test on 1 December. Ten testers opt in on 1 December and two more opt in on 4 December. The twelfth person reaches 14 consecutive days on 18 December, so that is your earliest apply date, not 15 December. If one of the first ten leaves on 10 December and a replacement opts in on 11 December, the replacement reaches day 14 on 25 December and your date moves to 25 December, unless you had spare testers. With 15 testers, the same dropout changes nothing.

### What pushes the date back

- Slow opt-ins. A tester who is invited but does not opt in has no clock running.
- Opting out and back in. Google says the 14 days must be consecutive, so a tester who opts out and rejoins starts again.
- Falling below 12. Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out do not count.
- Low engagement. Google lists fewer than 12 opted-in testers or insufficient tester engagement as reasons you may need to continue the closed test.
- Applying too early. Apply only when 12 testers have each passed 14 consecutive days.

### How to make the date as early as possible

1. Recruit 15 testers, not 12, so a dropout does not move your date.
2. Get all testers to opt in on day 0 or day 1. Send the opt-in link with one clear instruction.
3. Ask testers to open the app on most days and to try a feature, so engagement looks like real use.
4. Ship a small update during the test to give testers a reason to open the app again.
5. Prepare your answers for the production form while the test runs: what you tested, the feedback you got and what you changed.

### Finding the 12 testers

If you have no friends with Android phones, you can get testers on Tester Exchange. Testers are real people on their own phones and each day they open your app is recorded. You can test other developers' apps free at https://testerexchange.com/earn in your phone's browser, and each app you test brings a tester to yours, or pay once for 12, 15 or 25 testers. Dropouts are replaced automatically, so your count stays above 12.

### Frequently asked questions

**Can I apply on day 14 of the closed test?** Only if all 12 testers opted in on day 0. Each tester needs 14 consecutive days from their own opt-in date.

**How long does Google take to review a production access application?** Google says review usually takes seven days or less, but can occasionally take longer.

**Does this rule apply to my account?** Google's help page applies it to personal developer accounts created after 13 November 2023.

**What if a tester leaves before day 14?** Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days and then opt out do not count, so replace them quickly.

**Where is the Apply for production button?** On the Dashboard in Play Console, once the criteria are met.
